analysis.one_liner: Restores taxes on polluting industries to fund toxic waste site cleanup.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have reinstated expired taxes on oil and chemical companies to pay for cleaning up toxic waste sites, never received a committee vote and died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since the mid-1990s, the trust fund that pays to clean up the nation's worst toxic waste sites has been funded by general taxpayer money instead of the taxes on oil, chemical, and other corporations that were allowed to expire. This bill would have brought those taxes back through the end of 2018: an excise tax on hazardous substances (including petroleum) and a corporate environmental income tax. Cleanup of sites like Superfund locations would once again be paid for primarily by the industries whose pollution created the sites, rather than by general taxpayers.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near toxic waste sites, since a dedicated, polluter-funded trust fund means more cleanups can proceed without being limited by general tax revenue. Ordinary taxpayers also benefit, because they stop covering cleanup costs that polluting industries once paid.

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, an excise tax on hazardous substances including petroleum, through January 1, 2019, to finance the Superfund trust fund.
Reinstates the corporate environmental income tax, a tax on large corporations, for the same period, restoring the polluter-pays funding structure that lapsed in the 1990s.
Removes export provisions so the petroleum excise tax applies to crude oil regardless of whether it is exported, closing a gap that would otherwise let companies avoid the tax.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and chemical companies and other corporations that would pay the reinstated excise and corporate taxes. Some of those costs could be passed along to consumers in the price of fuel and petroleum-based products, which is the standard incidence of an excise tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, chemical, and other large corporations

drawbacks.text: The excise tax applies to petroleum and petroleum products, so some of the cost would likely show up in higher prices for gasoline and petroleum-based products.
The bill raises federal revenue permanently until 2019 without any offsetting cuts, which supporters of lower overall taxation would oppose as a tax increase.
The reinstated taxes run through 2019 only, so Congress would face the same lapse again afterward unless it extended them again.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted and concrete: communities stuck with toxic waste sites get a funded cleanup program paid for by the industries responsible for the pollution. The costs are broad but modest per household, spread across consumers as slightly higher fuel and chemical-product prices. On balance this is a well-established, widely praised policy design (polluter pays) whose main weakness is the sunset date, not the mechanism.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Frank Pallone introduced the bill on May 23, 2013, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
That referral was the bill's only action; no markup, vote, or further consideration ever occurred.
The 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, chemical, and other large corporations that would have paid the reinstated taxes kept that money, while the cost of cleaning up existing toxic waste sites continues to fall on general taxpayers instead of the industries whose pollution created the sites.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to reinstate Superfund financing taxes and referred it to committee.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Petroleum and chemical industry lobbying
against.role: Industry groups representing companies that would pay the reinstated Superfund taxes
against.what_they_did: Opposed reinstatement of the Superfund taxes that expired in the mid-1990s.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only two sponsors were both Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor ever joined; no votes were taken, so the partisan split was never formally tested.

industries.note: The reinstated excise tax applies to petroleum and crude oil, with the export exemption removed, so refiners would pay a per-barrel tax they have avoided since the 1990s. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against communities whose tax dollars now cover toxic cleanup.

The bill reinstates both the hazardous substance excise tax and the corporate environmental income tax, shifting cleanup costs back onto chemical companies that originally benefited from the tax lapse. Meanwhile, toxic waste remediation is financed by the general taxpayer instead.
The corporate environmental income tax applies to corporations' taxable income, so the corporate sector broadly would pay toward Superfund cleanup rather than it coming from general revenue.
